strengths: Significance: A compact, reusable encoder for time-series classification is useful. Mantis reports the highest mean accuracy among the evaluated foundation models on UCR-128, UEA-27, HAR, and EEG. Table 1 reports 0.8195 on UCR and 0.7420 on UEA, with only 2.2M parameters after truncation.

Soundness: The tokenizer ablations are reasonably informative. Appendix B.2 includes a duplicated signal branch to distinguish the contribution of first-order differences from increased capacity. Separate experiments examine patch statistics, pooling, kernel size, positional encoding, augmentation, and pre-training objectives.

Originality: The strongest contribution is the empirical investigation of intermediate representations in compact time-series models. The layer-by-epoch analysis and the additional 100K-sample, 1,000-epoch experiment provide useful evidence that training duration affects which layers transfer best.

Evaluation and presentation: The manuscript is generally readable and includes extensive per-dataset results, several baseline families, and domain-shift evaluations. Improving competing models through intermediate-layer extraction and strengthening Catch22 are welcome efforts to avoid weak comparisons.

Limitations and ethics: The authors acknowledge inconsistent self-ensembling benefits, limitations of channel-independent processing, and architecture-related confounding in the reconstruction-objective ablation. Synthetic pre-training reduces direct corpus-overlap and privacy concerns; no material ethical violation is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—model selection is insufficiently separated from evaluation. Section 4.1 selects layers by their highest downstream performance, and Appendix B repeatedly uses UCR accuracy to choose architecture, aggregation, and other configurations. The manuscript does not establish that these decisions use training-only validation or a separate development benchmark. This leaves a substantial risk of benchmark-selection bias in the central UCR claims. Synthetic pre-training prevents direct pre-training overlap but does not resolve downstream test-set tuning. A clearly specified selection protocol and untouched evaluation are needed.

Reproducibility—essential pre-training details are missing. The paper specifies the contrastive temperature and cropping range, but not the pre-training optimizer, learning rate and schedule, batch size, complete projector configuration, or precise CauKer generation settings. It also does not clearly identify the final checkpoint's data size and training duration. Appendix C supplies fine-tuning settings, which do not substitute for the pre-training recipe. The sources of randomness underlying reported standard deviations also need clarification.

Significance—the broad state-of-the-art framing exceeds the comparisons. The supervised baselines in Appendix D are largely older methods; strong contemporary time-series classifiers such as MiniRocket/MultiRocket and HIVE-COTE 2.0 are absent. Comparisons with frozen foundation models are valuable, but do not establish superiority over specialized classification methods. The UCR-91 improvement over TS2Vec is only 0.68 percentage points, with no paired uncertainty analysis establishing how reliable that advantage is.

Evaluation consistency and reporting need correction. The study switches from standardized logistic regression on UCR-91 to random forests elsewhere, but does not substantiate the claim that this preserves relative rankings. Table 17 also reproduces identical TNC and TS-TCC results throughout, including their aggregate accuracy, raising a concrete concern about baseline transcription. These issues require an audit before relying on the headline comparisons.

Originality and interpretation: Most ingredients are established techniques, including InfoNCE, CauKer synthetic data, scalar encoding, intermediate-layer extraction, and embedding concatenation. The useful contribution is their combination and empirical analysis, rather than a fundamentally new learning method. Claims about scaling laws and final-layer overfitting are stronger than the evidence: the experiments cover one compact architecture and a limited data range, and poorer downstream transfer alone does not establish overfitting of the pre-training objective.

Efficiency and terminology: Runtime comparisons omit hardware details and compare encoder feature extraction with tabular models performing supervised prediction, without consistently including downstream classifier fitting. Parameter count alone does not establish deployment memory requirements, particularly with channel concatenation and ensembles. Also, although explicitly defined, calling supervised probing 'zero-shot' is misleading; most experiments use a nonlinear random forest rather than linear probing. These distinctions should be reflected consistently in the claims.

strengths: Significance: A compact, reusable encoder for time series classification is practically useful. Table 1 reports higher average accuracy for Mantis than the evaluated foundation models on UCR-128 (0.8195) and UEA-27 (0.7420), with further encouraging results on HAR and EEG. The pruned encoder has only 2.2 million parameters.

Soundness: The extensive ablations investigate meaningful alternatives, including tokenizer branches, duplicated signal branches as a capacity control, pre-training objectives, augmentations, output aggregation, and synthetic versus real pre-training data. Table 7 provides useful evidence that synthetic pre-training can compete with substantially larger real-data corpora.

Originality: Although many components are established, their integration into a compact classification encoder is useful. The layer-by-layer analysis provides an interesting empirical observation: intermediate representations can improve with additional pre-training even when final-layer transfer performance stagnates. The matched-update experiment in Appendix B.3 strengthens this analysis.

Presentation: The architecture and feature-extraction pipeline are generally understandable, and the appendix supplies extensive per-dataset results. The authors acknowledge that self-ensembling does not improve UCR-91, that reconstruction objectives may be disadvantaged by the architecture, and that independent channel processing has limitations.

Research ethics: Synthetic pre-training reduces direct benchmark-overlap and pre-training privacy concerns. The evaluation uses existing datasets, acknowledges the Ego4D licensing requirement, and includes several domain-shift evaluations. I found no material ethical violation established by the manuscript.
weaknesses: Soundness—model selection is insufficiently specified. Section 4.1 selects layers by their highest downstream performance, while Appendix B uses UCR accuracy to compare layers, epochs, kernel sizes, architectures, augmentations, and aggregation strategies. The paper does not identify a separate validation protocol or held-out development collection for these choices. Consequently, readers cannot determine whether the reported UCR results are independent of model selection. This is a central concern, rather than proof of test leakage: the selection procedure needs to be documented and evaluated with an untouched test protocol. Synthetic pre-training alone does not resolve this issue.

Reproducibility is materially incomplete. The manuscript specifies fine-tuning hyperparameters but does not provide an equivalent complete pre-training recipe: optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch size, weight decay, projector configuration, and CauKer generation settings are missing or insufficiently specified. The exact data size and checkpoint underlying the headline results are also not clearly connected to the reported ablations. Hardware and timing methodology are insufficiently documented. These omissions prevent reliable reconstruction of the central contribution from the manuscript.

Significance—the broad state-of-the-art and specialized-method comparison claims exceed the evaluation. Appendix D adds several older supervised baselines, but strong contemporary time series classifiers such as ROCKET-family methods and HIVE-COTE are absent. Comparisons against foundation models support a narrower claim about frozen feature extraction; they do not establish general classification superiority or that the gap to strong specialized approaches has been closed.

Soundness—the statistical support for superiority is limited. The UCR-91 advantage over TS2Vec is 0.8584 versus 0.8516, but the manuscript supplies no paired uncertainty analysis across datasets. Some results include variability, yet its source and the replication protocol are not consistently explained. Replacing logistic regression with random forests in Section 4.2 also changes the evaluation substantially; the assertion that relative rankings are unaffected is not demonstrated through a controlled comparison on the same collection.

Originality and interpretation: Contrastive learning, crop-resize augmentation, statistical encodings, intermediate-layer extraction, and embedding concatenation are largely established techniques, several explicitly borrowed from cited work. The contribution is principally their integration and empirical analysis. Claims that synthetic data are out-of-distribution 'by construction,' that final layers overfit the contrastive objective, and that the findings establish a route to scaling laws are stronger than the evidence: non-overlapping data provenance does not establish distribution shift, and downstream accuracy curves do not directly diagnose objective overfitting or establish a scaling law.

Presentation and efficiency claims need tighter qualification. The paper explicitly defines its terminology, but calling supervised classifier fitting 'zero-shot' remains liable to misinterpretation, and calling the broader setup 'linear probing' is inaccurate for random forests. Figure 4 describes Mantis as the most lightweight model although Table 6 lists pruned NuTime at 2.0M parameters versus 2.2M for Mantis. Forward-pass timing also omits downstream classifier costs and does not establish end-to-end resource requirements for multichannel inputs or cross-model fusion. Overall, the useful empirical results do not outweigh the unresolved evaluation and reproducibility weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: A compact, reusable time-series classifier is practically valuable. Mantis reports higher average accuracy than the evaluated foundation models on UCR, UEA-27, HAR, and EEG, while requiring only 2.2M parameters after truncation. Table 1 reports 0.8195 on UCR and 0.7420 on UEA-27.

Soundness: The ablations meaningfully investigate the tokenizer, augmentation, pretraining objective, intermediate layers, and output aggregation. The duplicated signal branch in Figure 8 helps distinguish the benefit of differencing from simply adding parameters. The update-matched experiment in Figure 13 also strengthens the intermediate-layer analysis.

Originality: Although most components have precedents, their integration is useful. The observation that intermediate representations benefit more from increased synthetic pretraining data than final-layer representations provides an interesting empirical contribution.

Presentation and evaluation: The method is generally understandable, with clear architectural diagrams and extensive per-dataset results. Applying intermediate-layer analysis to competing models and strengthening Catch22 are constructive efforts toward competitive baselines.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript acknowledges channel-independent processing limitations, the lack of self-ensembling improvement on UCR-91, and architectural confounding in reconstruction-objective comparisons. Synthetic pretraining reduces direct pretraining-corpus contamination and privacy concerns; no material ethical violation is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—model selection is insufficiently separated from evaluation. Section 4.1 selects layers by their highest downstream performance, while Appendix B selects architecture, kernel size, aggregation, and other choices using UCR accuracy. The manuscript does not specify a held-out validation procedure for these decisions. Consequently, readers cannot determine whether the headline UCR results are independent test estimates or reflect repeated benchmark-level selection. Synthetic pretraining does not resolve this issue. A documented validation-only selection protocol and evaluation on untouched datasets are needed.

Reproducibility—essential pretraining details are missing. The paper specifies the contrastive temperature and augmentation range but does not clearly provide the pretraining optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch size, projector architecture, precise CauKer generation configuration, or an unambiguous final checkpoint recipe. Fine-tuning details in Appendix C do not fill these gaps. The abstract's source-code link is blank in the supplied manuscript, preventing verification through the promised implementation.

Significance—the broad state-of-the-art and specialized-method comparison claims exceed the evidence. The additional supervised baselines in Appendix D are largely older methods; strong contemporary time-series classifiers such as ROCKET-family methods and HIVE-COTE 2.0 are absent. The experiments establish competitiveness against the included foundation models, but not general state-of-the-art classification performance.

Statistical support is incomplete. Several headline improvements are modest: UCR-91 accuracy is 0.8584 for Mantis versus 0.8516 for TS2Vec, and fusion reaches 0.8620. Per-dataset standard deviations are useful, but aggregate paired uncertainty or significance analysis is absent, and the source of randomness is not consistently specified. Claims of significant superiority therefore need stronger support.

Presentation and claim precision: Calling supervised probing 'zero-shot' is nonstandard even with the explicit definition, and much of the evaluation uses random forests rather than linear probing. Frozen-encoder transfer would describe the setting more accurately. Likewise, synthetic data are not necessarily out-of-distribution by construction, and the limited data-scaling experiments do not establish scaling laws.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete. The runtime study omits hardware details and focuses on forward-pass timing for synthetic univariate inputs of length 100. It does not establish end-to-end downstream cost, including classifier fitting and high-dimensional multichannel embeddings. Parameter counts support compactness, but deployment-efficiency claims require more representative measurements.
